headline: Google Takes Over a Giant Computer Center Project in Wyoming

levels.label: Grade 3-4
levels.summary: A company called Crusoe builds huge buildings full of computers called data centers. These buildings help power things like apps, websites, and artificial intelligence, which is computer technology that can "think" and answer questions. Crusoe was building a giant data center in Wyoming, but it was taking too long and costing too much money. So Crusoe sold the unfinished project to Google, a much bigger company. Google plans to spend $17 billion, which is an enormous amount of money, to finish building it. Even though Google took over this project, the two companies are still working together on another data center in Texas. This story shows that building these giant computer centers is very hard work. It takes a lot of planning, money, and time, and sometimes even big, well-funded companies run into trouble and need help finishing the job. More of these computer centers are being built because people use AI more and more every day.

levels.label: Grade 5-6
levels.summary: Crusoe is a company that builds data centers, which are large buildings packed with powerful computers. These computers help run websites, apps, and artificial intelligence (AI) programs that can answer questions or create images. Last year, Crusoe started building a massive data center in Wyoming, hoping to grow it into one of the biggest in the world. However, the project ran into problems with cost and how long it was taking to finish. Google, a huge tech company, had actually wanted to be a customer at this data center but decided not to work with Crusoe on it. Instead, Google ended up buying the whole unfinished project and plans to spend $17 billion to complete it themselves. Even after this, Crusoe and Google are still partners on a different data center being built in Texas. This event shows how difficult and expensive it is to build the giant computer facilities that power today's AI boom. Even well-funded, successful companies can struggle to finish these massive projects on time. Despite this setback, Crusoe is still doing well overall — the company raised about $3.9 billion from investors just months after the Wyoming deal became public, and it continues to build data centers for other major companies like Microsoft, Meta, and OpenAI.

levels.label: Grade 7-8
levels.summary: Crusoe, a data center company based in Denver, recently sold an unfinished data center project in Wyoming to Google. Data centers are large facilities filled with powerful computers and GPUs (graphics processing units), special computer chips that are especially good at running artificial intelligence programs. As AI has become more popular, tech companies have been racing to build bigger and bigger data centers to keep up with demand. Crusoe had announced the Wyoming project last year with plans to eventually make it enormous — capable of using 10 gigawatts of electricity, an amount that could power millions of homes. However, the project ran into trouble. Google, which had originally considered becoming a customer there, reportedly grew concerned about how much the project was costing and how long it was taking to build. Rather than sign on as a customer, Google decided to buy the entire project from Crusoe and finish it themselves, planning to invest $17 billion in the site. Neither company revealed exactly how much Google paid Crusoe for the land and partially built structures. This situation shows a bigger challenge in the tech industry: even well-funded companies can struggle to build massive data centers on schedule and within budget, partly because of difficulties getting equipment and electrical power, and partly because local communities sometimes push back against these huge construction projects. Despite losing the Wyoming project, Crusoe hasn't been pushed out of the AI infrastructure business. The company is still building a separate data center for Google in Texas, and it continues major projects for companies like Oracle, OpenAI, Microsoft, and Meta. Just months after the Wyoming sale became public, Crusoe raised $3.9 billion from investors, suggesting that despite this setback, people still believe strongly in the company's future in the booming data center industry.

levels.label: Grade 9-10
levels.summary: Crusoe, an eight-year-old data center developer based in Denver that was recently valued at $30.9 billion, has confirmed it sold an unfinished data center project in southeastern Wyoming to Google. The sale marks a significant setback for Crusoe, but it also reveals just how competitive and demanding the race to build AI infrastructure has become. Data centers are massive facilities packed with servers and specialized computer chips called GPUs, which power everything from AI chatbots to cloud computing services. As demand for AI has exploded, companies like Google, Microsoft, and Meta have needed exponentially more computing power, driving a construction boom in data centers across the country. Crusoe originally announced the Wyoming project last year in partnership with Tallgrass, a Blackstone-backed infrastructure company, with ambitions to eventually scale it up to 10 gigawatts of power capacity — an almost unprecedented size for a single site. Google had considered becoming a customer there but reportedly backed out after raising concerns about the project's rising costs and slipping construction timeline. Rather than walk away entirely, Google chose to buy the unfinished site outright and take over construction itself, committing $17 billion to complete the campus. Neither company has disclosed the sale price of the original deal. This outcome highlights a broader industry problem: even well-capitalized, experienced developers can struggle to deliver data centers on time and within budget, often due to supply chain issues, equipment shortages, strained power grids, and resistance from local communities worried about land use, water consumption, or noise. Despite this high-profile stumble, Crusoe's relationship with Google hasn't ended — the two companies are still partnering on a separate data center project near Amarillo, Texas. Crusoe also remains deeply involved in the AI boom elsewhere, building large campuses for Oracle, OpenAI, and Microsoft in Abilene, Texas, and reportedly signing a $13 billion, five-year cloud computing deal with the trading firm Jane Street. Notably, the Wyoming setback didn't shake investor confidence: Crusoe raised a $3.9 billion funding round in September, shortly after news of the Google sale became public, and added new board members, including entrepreneur JB Straubel. The episode illustrates both the enormous financial stakes of the AI infrastructure race and the operational risks even successful companies face when trying to build at an unprecedented scale and speed.

levels.label: Grade 11+
levels.summary: Crusoe, a Denver-based data center developer recently valued at $30.9 billion, has confirmed the sale of an unfinished data center project in southeastern Wyoming to Google — a deal that underscores both the staggering financial stakes and the operational fragility of the current AI infrastructure boom. Data centers, the physical backbone of cloud computing and artificial intelligence, require enormous amounts of electricity, specialized hardware like GPUs (graphics processing units optimized for AI workloads), and complex logistics to construct at scale. As AI adoption has accelerated, tech giants have been locked in an infrastructure arms race, competing to secure the computing capacity needed to train and run increasingly powerful AI models. Crusoe had announced the Wyoming project last year in partnership with Tallgrass, a Blackstone-backed infrastructure firm, with plans to eventually expand it to a massive 10 gigawatts of power capacity. Google had initially been courted as a potential customer for the site but ultimately declined, reportedly due to concerns about ballooning costs and delays in the construction timeline under Crusoe's management. Rather than abandon the site, Google opted to acquire the unfinished project directly, pledging $17 billion toward its completion — though the purchase price Google paid Crusoe remains undisclosed. This transaction illustrates a structural challenge facing independent data center developers: even well-funded, experienced firms can struggle to execute multibillion-dollar projects on schedule, hampered by supply chain bottlenecks, grid capacity constraints, and increasingly organized local opposition to large-scale construction projects that consume significant land, water, and power resources. Yet the setback has not meaningfully dented Crusoe's broader standing in the industry. The company continues to develop a separate data center for Google near Amarillo, Texas, suggesting the relationship between the two companies remains intact despite the Wyoming stumble. Crusoe's portfolio includes some of the most significant AI infrastructure contracts in the industry: a phased campus in Abilene, Texas, serving Oracle and OpenAI; an adjacent 900-megawatt facility for Microsoft slated to begin operating in mid-2027; and a reported $13 billion, five-year cloud computing agreement with trading firm Jane Street. Meta is also listed among its customers. Notably, just months after news of the Google deal first broke, Crusoe closed a $3.9 billion funding round and added new board members, including JB Straubel, the Redwood Materials founder and Tesla board member who first invested in Crusoe in 2021. Founded by Chase Lochmiller and Cully Cavness as a cryptocurrency-mining operation that repurposed natural gas otherwise burned off as waste, Crusoe has since transformed into a major player in AI infrastructure. The Wyoming sale, then, is less a sign of the company's decline than a case study in the volatility and complexity of building the physical infrastructure that underpins the modern AI economy — where even sophisticated developers can misjudge costs and timelines, and where the largest tech companies are increasingly willing to step in and take direct control when stakes are high enough.

questions: Data centers use huge amounts of electricity and water. How do you think building more of them near towns and cities might affect the people who live there, including your own community?

Why do you think a giant company like Google decided to buy and finish this project itself instead of just waiting for Crusoe to fix the delays? What does that tell you about how important AI technology has become to big companies?

As AI tools become part of daily life, like the ones used in schools or apps you might use, what trade-offs do you think are worth it to build the technology that powers them, and what trade-offs might not be worth it?
